tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

1	# The RL training signal as a feedback channel: limits from falsifiable axioms
2	
3	Draft 0.1 — 2026-10-12.
4	
5	This note types the reinforcement-learning paradigm in the
6	[evaluation design calculus](evaluation_design_calculus.md) and the
7	[feedback insertions](evaluation_feedback_insertions.md), states the
8	assumptions the paradigm's gains rest on as axioms, and derives from each
9	axiom an exact limit with the observation that would falsify the axiom. The
10	fixtures are in `src/spiral_ln/evaluation_feedback_signal.py`; the receipt
11	is under `output/evaluation_feedback_signal/`. No model was called.
12	
13	Three companion notes carry the pieces delegated to separate runs:
14	[partial leakage as a lattice](evaluation_feedback_lattice.md),
15	[the selection gap across generations](evaluation_feedback_multigen.md), and
16	[Feedback's composition laws](evaluation_feedback_composition.md).
17	
18	## 1. The question
19	
20	The claim under test is the one Will Brown and Prime Intellect have argued
21	for publicly: that gains in agent capability come from reinforcement learning
22	on environments, that environments are the bottleneck, and that the same
23	environment abstraction serves evals, RL and data generation. His position
24	on compounding is narrower than the claim is sometimes read: in a July 2026
25	post he argued that architectures, optimizers, kernels and algorithms each
26	sit on a sigmoid, and that figures like a thousandfold R&D speedup are too
27	loosely defined to assess; in a May 2025 interview he said evals saturate
28	and always need replacing, that deterministic rewards are painful to build,
29	and that model-based judges are underexplored. His posts from 12 October
30	2026 could not be read from this session, so nothing below quotes them.
31	
32	The dependency the note works along: RL gains depend on the training
33	signal; the training signal is a judgment fed back to the controller; a
34	judgment fed back is the calculus's `Feedback` operator, whose source set,
35	access class and ledger are declarable. So the paradigm's limits are
36	statements about a declared channel, and they can be checked from the
37	declaration without access to the model.
38	
39	## 2. Typing RL in the calculus
40	
41	An RL environment is an evaluation record \(\mathcal E=\langle
42	G,\Pi,D,Z,J,\mathcal A,C\rangle\) in which \(J\) is written back into
43	\(\Pi\) each generation:
44	
45	\[
46	\text{RL on } D_{\text{train}}
47	= \operatorname{Repeat}_{G}\big(\operatorname{Feedback}_{D_{\text{train}},\,q}\big).
48	\]
49	
50	Two access classes are in play, at different grains.
51	
52	- **Episode grain.** The loop sees each episode's reward, so on the training
53	  set \(q=\text{item\_level}\): every RL run is item-level feedback on its
54	  training distribution. A run that sees only batch means is score-only.
55	- **Step grain.** Within an episode of \(T\) steps the reward is a channel
56	  on the step-outcome record \(r\in\{0,1\}^T\). Outcome reward is the
57	  two-block partition \(\{r=1^T\}\) against the rest; partial credit is the
58	  Hamming weight; a verifier that stops at the first error reports the
59	  position of the first zero; a process reward is the record itself.
60	
61	`TrainingSignal.feedback_signature()` renders a declared setup in these
62	terms. Verifiable rewards are the case \(J\) deterministic and exact;
63	learned judges are the case \(J\) noisy, with an error rate and a share of
64	errors it has in common with the controller.
65	
66	## 3. Axioms
67	
68	Each is a condition the paradigm's reported gains rest on, and each names
69	the observation that would falsify it.
70	
71	| | Axiom | Falsified by |
72	|---|---|---|
73	| A1 | The loop reads \(J\) only through the declared channel at the declared access class. | A ledger breach; or item-level knowledge shown with fewer score queries than L2 allows. |
74	| A2 | The judge's errors are independent of the controller's. | Observed accuracy at or above the noise ceiling with patch share below the L3 threshold; or a measured \(\varepsilon_1>\varepsilon\). |
75	| A3 | The readout set never feeds the loop. | A ledger breach on the readout set. |
76	| A4 | A patch changes one item's outcome and no other. | Collateral outcome changes on unpatched items (the nearest-neighbour simulation in `output/eval_reuse_toys/` showed them). |
77	| A5 | Candidates have equal true value (the null for selection inflation). | A measured gain on a sealed readout. |
78	
79	A5 is the null hypothesis, not a belief; the inflation derived from it is
80	the part of a reported gain that needs no true gain to explain.
81	
82	## 4. Limits
83	
84	**L1. Bits per episode.** A deterministic channel with \(m\) images gives
85	at most \(\log_2 m\) bits per episode about the step record. Outcome reward
86	has \(m=2\); partial credit and first-failure have \(m=T+1\); process reward
87	has \(m=2^T\). To distinguish \(H\) hypotheses the loop needs at least
88	\(\lceil\log H/\log m\rceil\) episodes of that channel. For \(T=3\) steps,
89	identifying which steps fail (eight hypotheses) takes at least three
90	outcome-reward episodes and one process-reward episode. Partial credit and
91	first-failure are incomparable: neither factors through the other. Proof:
92	counting; `refines` checks factorization. *Finite verified example* for
93	\(T\le5\); the counting bound is an *algebraic identity*.
94	
95	**L2. Score-only is item-level after finitely many queries.** Let the loop
96	test a patch on any subset of the \(n\) selection items and read the set's
97	score. Once it knows the failure count \(f\), each query returns one of
98	\(f+1\) values, so \(q\) queries distinguish at most \((f+1)^q\) of the
99	\(\binom nf\) failure sets. Hence
100	\[
101	q_{\min}(n,f)\ \ge\ \Big\lceil \log\tbinom nf\big/\log(f+1)\Big\rceil ,
102	\]
103	and recursive halving identifies the set in at most \(f\lceil\log_2
104	n\rceil+1\) queries. `exact_min_queries` computes the minimax value
105	exhaustively for \(n\le7\); it lies between the bound and the halving count
106	in every cell, and equals \(\lceil\log_2n\rceil\) for one failure. The
107	ledger's `score_queries` count therefore bounds the leak: below
108	\(q_{\min}\) the loop cannot have identified the failed items; above the
109	halving count a set declared score-only should be treated as item-level.
110	Between the two the loop sits somewhere in the lattice of partial leaks of
111	the companion note, which prices each position: with per-category failure
112	counts, the patches needed to reach the ceiling fall monotonically as the
113	categories refine, from \(\tfrac8{13}\) of the set at one category to
114	\(\tfrac4{25}\) at singletons, with the exact expected-value formula and
115	greedy optimality proven. One more result from that note bears on
116	disclosure: the channel induced by two category maps observed together is
117	strictly finer than the join of the two channels observed separately, so a
118	ledger must record what the loop saw jointly, not the partitions one at a
119	time; the two agree exactly when the intersection graph of the two category
120	maps is a forest. *Finite verified example*; the lower bound is an
121	*algebraic identity*.
122	
123	**L3. Noise ceiling and its blind range.** From the insertions: with judge
124	error \(\varepsilon\) and base observed accuracy \(v\), a ceiling check is
125	silent until a share \((1-\varepsilon-v)/(1-v)\) of the set is memorized at
126	random, or \(1-\varepsilon-v\) of the set is patched on failures. Under A1
127	and A2 a reported training score above \(1-\varepsilon\) is evidence of
128	memorization past that share.
129	
130	**L4. A judge that shares errors with the judged.** Let the judge be wrong
131	with probability \(\varepsilon_0\) on items the controller gets right and
132	\(\varepsilon_1\) on items it gets wrong, with marginal
133	\(\varepsilon=a\varepsilon_0+(1-a)\varepsilon_1\). Observed accuracy is
134	\[
135	a(1-\varepsilon_0)+(1-a)\varepsilon_1
136	= a-\varepsilon+2(1-a)\varepsilon_1 ,
137	\]
138	which exceeds the independent-judge value by exactly
139	\(2(1-a)(\varepsilon_1-\varepsilon)\), and reaches the ceiling
140	\(1-\varepsilon\) exactly when \(\varepsilon_1\ge\tfrac12\), whatever
141	\(a\) and \(\varepsilon\). Feasibility caps \(\varepsilon_1\) at
142	\(\varepsilon/(1-a)\), so the ceiling is reachable without memorization iff
143	\(\varepsilon\ge(1-a)/2\): the judge must be wrong at least half as often
144	as the controller. In the fixture (\(a=\tfrac45\), \(\varepsilon=\tfrac1{10}\))
145	the independent judge reports \(\tfrac{37}{50}\); the most correlated
146	feasible judge reports \(\tfrac9{10}\), the ceiling, an inflation of
147	\(\tfrac4{25}\). So L3's check has a confound: a score at the ceiling is
148	memorization under A2, and A2 is what a learned judge trained on the
149	controller's outputs most plausibly violates. *Algebraic identity*, checked
150	on a rational grid.
151	
152	**L5. Running-maximum inflation under reuse.** Under A5, keeping the best
153	of \(K\) candidates scored on a reused set overstates by the one-generation
154	gap of the selection law. Across \(G\) generations with the incumbent kept
155	and \(K\) fresh candidates each generation, the reported count is the
156	maximum of \(GK+1\) i.i.d. draws, so the gap is `selection_inflation(n,
157	GK+1, p)`: non-decreasing in \(G\), with diminishing increments, rising
158	toward \(1-p\) for fixed \(n\) and never stationary. (The composition note's
159	two-generation fixture carries the incumbent into a pool of \(K-1\) fresh
160	candidates and so reaches \(2K-1\) draws; the two conventions agree once the
161	pool size is fixed.) At \(p=\tfrac12\), \(n=8\), \(K=2\) the gap runs
162	\(0.147,\ 0.273,\ 0.321,\ 0.365\) at \(G=1,5,10,20\). Fresh blocks remove
163	the accumulation: a separate readout block gives gap zero, and reporting on
164	the selection block gives the one-generation gap at every generation. A
165	gate that accepts only gains above a noise margin lowers the gap under the
166	null, by a coupling argument, but the ordering can reverse once candidates
167	carry true gains, because the gate refuses those too. The companion
168	multi-generation note proves these as a Markov chain on the score lattice,
169	and finds that the simulations' "late gains look larger than they are"
170	prediction was a property of their decaying gain schedule, not of reuse.
171	*Algebraic identity* for the chain results; *synthetic mechanism result*
172	for the drift cells.
173	
174	**L6. Finer feedback is worth at least as much.** For the loop's decision
175	of which candidate to keep, with any prior over candidate types and any
176	utility, the Bayes value under channel \(g\) is at least the value under
177	any \(f\) that factors through \(g\): a decision rule on \(f\)-images is a
178	decision rule on \(g\)-images. This is the garbling direction of
179	Blackwell's ordering. For incomparable channels each can be worth more:
180	partial credit beats first-failure when types differ in how many steps fail,
181	and loses when they differ in which step fails first. With exchangeable
182	steps partial credit is sufficient, so it ties process reward and beats
183	first-failure. *Algebraic identity* for the inequality; *finite verified
184	example* for the strict cases, cross-checked by enumerating every decision
185	rule.
186	
187	## 5. What this says about the paradigm claim
188	
189	Decompose "RL on environments keeps yielding gains" into the conditions
190	under which the reported gains are not phantom.
191	
192	1. **Supply.** Fresh sealed items arrive at least as fast as the loop
193	   consumes them. Otherwise L2 turns score-only reuse into item-level reuse
194	   and L5 adds a running-maximum gap to every reported score. The
195	   environments-hub programme is a bet on this condition; the ledger
196	   quantities that test it are `score_queries` and `distinct_patched` per
197	   set, against the set's size, and the joint channel through which any
198	   category-level signal reached the loop. The composition note adds that
199	   the ledger is the only place this is visible: an offline rescoring of the
200	   readout set moves the readout gap by the same amount as a memorizing
201	   feedback step and leaves no other trace.
202	2. **Signal width.** The reward channel is fine enough for the credit the
203	   task needs. L1 says outcome reward supplies one bit an episode; process
204	   and turn-level rewards widen the channel, but every widening past a
205	   deterministic verifier needs a judge, which brings in the next condition.
206	3. **Judge independence.** L4 says a judge that shares half its errors with
207	   the controller reports the ceiling for a controller that has learned
208	   nothing. A learned judge trained on the same data as the controller, or
209	   on the controller's outputs, is the case where A2 is least plausible, and
210	   it is the case the interview called underexplored.
211	
212	None of L1–L6 bounds the true gain available from fresh environments with
213	exact verifiers. The limits say where a reported gain can come from without
214	a true one, and what has to be published to rule that out: the set sizes,
215	the access class, the query and patch counts, the judge's error and shared
216	error rates, and the readout ledger. Of the five published claims in the
217	[atlas](rsi_claims_atlas.md), one publishes a readout at all and none
218	publishes the counts.
219	
220	The position in the July post, that every component sits on a sigmoid, is
221	consistent with these limits and not derived from them. What the limits add
222	is that the reported curve and the true curve separate under reuse and
223	under a correlated judge, so a sigmoid in the reported curve is not
224	evidence either way about the true one until the ledger is published.
225	
226	## 6. Not delivered
227	
228	- No observed controller, environment or judge. The fixtures are exact
229	  arithmetic on declared quantities.
230	- The step-level channels assume a binary outcome per step and a
231	  conjunctive task; graded or path-dependent rewards need their own
232	  partition.
233	- L2's query model lets the loop patch any subset. A loop that can only
234	  retrain, not patch, has a noisier channel; the bound still holds as a
235	  lower bound.
236	- L4 treats a binary judge. A graded judge with correlated errors needs the
237	  same decomposition on a larger alphabet.
238	- A measurement procedure for \(\varepsilon_1\): grade a sealed sample with
239	  an independent judge and compare error overlap. Proposed, not built.

23	## 1. Channels are partitions; the lattice data-processing law
24	
25	A deterministic feedback channel on records \(\{0,1\}^n\) is a function \(f\);
26	two channels carry the same information exactly when \(\ker f\) agrees, so a
27	channel *is* a partition of the record set. Convention: \(p\le q\) when \(q\)
28	refines \(p\); the one-block partition (`sealed`) is the bottom, the discrete
29	partition (`item_level`) the top, \(p\vee q\) the common refinement (observing
30	both) and \(p\wedge q\) the finest common coarsening (components of the union
31	of the two relations). This is the partition lattice, orientation reversed.
32	
33	**Proposition 1 (lattice data-processing law and converse).** For all
34	distributions \(P,Q\) on records, \(p\le q\) implies
35	\(\mathrm{TV}(p_\#P,p_\#Q)\le\mathrm{TV}(q_\#P,q_\#Q)\); and if \(p\not\le q\)
36	there are point masses \(P,Q\) reversing the inequality.
37	
38	*Proof.* \(\mathrm{TV}(p_\#P,p_\#Q)=\max_U|P(U)-Q(U)|\) over unions \(U\) of
39	blocks of \(p\). When \(q\) refines \(p\), every block of \(p\) is a union of
40	blocks of \(q\), so the maximum for \(p\) ranges over a subset of the sets
41	available to \(q\). If \(q\) does not refine \(p\), some block of \(q\) holds
42	\(x,y\) that \(p\) separates; \(P=\delta_x,Q=\delta_y\) give \(\mathrm{TV}\)
43	one through \(p\) and zero through \(q\). \(\square\)
44	
45	So \(\mathrm{TV}\) through \(p\vee q\) is at least the larger of the two and
46	through \(p\wedge q\) at most the smaller; the testbed's one-kernel contraction
47	is one comparable pair. *Evidence status: algebraic identity.* Fixture
48	`lattice_fixture(2, 2)`: all 15 partitions of \(\{0,1\}^2\), 225 ordered pairs,
49	100 pairs of grid distributions; the law holds on every comparable pair, fails
50	somewhere on every non-comparable pair, join and meet satisfy their lattice
51	definitions, and `access_kernel`'s three classes are bottom, middle, top.
52	
53	## 2. Category leakage is an order embedding, not a scale
54	
55	A category map, a partition \(\gamma\) of the items \([n]\), induces the channel
56	\(\Phi(\gamma)\): the per-category pass-count vector.
57	
58	**Proposition 2.** \(\Phi(\gamma)\le\Phi(\gamma')\) iff \(\gamma\le\gamma'\),
59	so \(\Phi\) is an order embedding; \(\Phi(\text{one block})=\)`score_only` and
60	\(\Phi(\text{singletons})=\)`item_level`.
61	
62	*Proof.* If \(\gamma'\) refines \(\gamma\), each \(\gamma\)-count is a sum of
63	\(\gamma'\)-counts, so equal \(\gamma'\)-counts force equal \(\gamma\)-counts.
64	If not, some \(\gamma'\)-block holds items \(i,j\) that \(\gamma\) separates;
65	the records failing only \(i\) and only \(j\) have equal \(\gamma'\)-counts and
66	unequal \(\gamma\)-counts. The endpoints are the definitions. \(\square\)
67	*Evidence status: algebraic identity*, checked exhaustively on all 5 maps of
68	\([3]\) and 15 maps of \([4]\) in `category_order_fixture`.
69	
70	The image is order-isomorphic to the partition lattice of \([n]\), not a chain
71	for \(n\ge3\), so "how much leaks" has no scalar. On \([3]\), with
72	\(A=\{0,1\}|\{2\}\) and \(B=\{0\}|\{1,2\}\): \(B\) separates "fail item 0" from
73	"fail item 1" (\(\mathrm{TV}=1\)) while \(A\) gives 0, and conversely for "fail 1" vs "fail 2".
74	
75	**Proposition 2b (meets are preserved).** \(\Phi(\gamma\wedge\gamma')=
76	\Phi(\gamma)\wedge\Phi(\gamma')\) for all \(\gamma,\gamma'\).
77	
78	*Proof.* \(\Phi\) is an order embedding, so \(\Phi(\gamma\wedge\gamma')\le
79	\Phi(\gamma)\wedge\Phi(\gamma')\). Conversely let \(r,s\) have equal pass
80	counts on every block of \(\gamma\wedge\gamma'\). Those blocks are the
81	connected components of the graph on items whose edges join two items lying
82	in a common \(\gamma\)-block or a common \(\gamma'\)-block. Swapping the bits
83	at two items of one \(\gamma\)-block preserves every \(\gamma\)-count, so a
84	record and its swap share a \(\Phi(\gamma)\)-block, hence a block of the
85	meet; likewise for \(\gamma'\). The edge transpositions of a connected graph
86	generate its symmetric group, so within each component every arrangement of
87	a fixed number of passes is reached from every other by such swaps. Hence
88	\(r\) and \(s\) share a block of the meet. \(\square\)
89	*Evidence status: algebraic identity*, checked on all 25, 225 and 2704
90	ordered pairs of maps on 3, 4 and 5 items (`category_lattice_fixture`).
91	
92	**Proposition 2c (joins are preserved iff the intersection graph is a
93	forest).** Let \(I(\gamma,\gamma')\) be the bipartite graph on the blocks of
94	\(\gamma\) and of \(\gamma'\) with an edge where two blocks intersect; its
95	edges are the cells of \(\gamma\vee\gamma'\). Then
96	\(\Phi(\gamma)\vee\Phi(\gamma')=\Phi(\gamma\vee\gamma')\) iff
97	\(I(\gamma,\gamma')\) is acyclic.
98	
99	*Proof.* \(\Phi(\gamma\vee\gamma')\) identifies records with equal cell
100	counts, \(\Phi(\gamma)\vee\Phi(\gamma')\) those with equal row and column
101	margins; cell counts determine margins, so the refined channel is always at
102	least as fine. If \(I\) has a cycle \(A_1B_1A_2B_2\cdots A_kB_k\), put one
103	pass in each cell \(A_i\cap B_i\) for one record and one in each
104	\(A_{i+1}\cap B_i\) for the other: every block on the cycle then holds
105	exactly one pass in both records, so the margins agree while the cells
106	differ. If \(I\) is a forest, peel leaves: a leaf block has a single
107	nonempty cell, whose count is that block's margin; remove it and recurse,
108	so the margins determine every cell. \(\square\)
109	
110	For rows \(\{0,1\}|\{2,3\}\) and columns \(\{0,2\}|\{1,3\}\) the graph is a
111	4-cycle and `1001`, `0110` is the witness: two separate category leaks are
112	strictly coarser than one leak with the refined categories. On \([4]\) the
113	six failing ordered pairs are the three pairings into two pairs taken
114	crosswise; on \([5]\) 210 of 2704 ordered pairs fail, and
115	`join_failure_witness` builds a valid witness from a cycle for each.
116	*Evidence status: algebraic identity*, checked exhaustively on 3, 4, 5 items.
117	
118	## 3. Cost of a leak, exact
119	
120	Setting of `noise_ceiling_fixture`: clean accuracy \(4/5\), flip \(1/10\), so
121	\(v=37/50\), ceiling \(9/10\); on \(n=50\) items 13 fail and \(H=8\) hits are
122	needed. Under \(\Phi(\gamma)\) the loop knows \((n_c,F_c)\) per category and
123	patches uniformly at random without replacement; a patch on a passed item gains nothing.
124	
125	**Proposition 3 (expected gain is exact; greedy is optimal).** The \(j\)-th
126	patch in category \(c\) hits with conditional probability
127	\((F_c-h)/(n_c-j+1)\) given \(h\) earlier hits, and with unconditional
128	probability \(F_c/n_c\) for every \(j\) (exchangeability). So \(m_c\) patches
129	hit exactly \(m_cF_c/n_c\) in expectation: the expected-value formula of the
130	insertions note is the hypergeometric mean, not an approximation. Every patch
131	in \(c\) has the same marginal value, so filling categories in decreasing order
132	of \(F_c/n_c\) maximizes expected hits at every patch count. *Algebraic
133	identity*; checked against every allocation and every patch order.
134	
135	**Proposition 4 (patches to the ceiling).** With \(c_1,c_2,\dots\) the greedy
136	order, \(j\) the first index with \(\sum_{i\le j}F_{c_i}\ge H\),
137	\(N_{<j}=\sum_{i<j}n_{c_i}\) and \(H_j=H-\sum_{i<j}F_{c_i}\in[1,F_{c_j}]\):
138	the expected score reaches the ceiling at \(m^*=N_{<j}+H_jn_{c_j}/F_{c_j}\),
139	and the realized score first reaches it at a stopping time \(T\) with
140	\(\mathbb E[T]=N_{<j}+H_j(n_{c_j}+1)/(F_{c_j}+1)\) (negative-hypergeometric
141	mean; earlier categories are patched completely, so their hits are fixed). Hence
142	\(m^*-\mathbb E[T]=H_j(n_{c_j}-F_{c_j})/(F_{c_j}(F_{c_j}+1))\in[0,m^*/(F_{c_j}+1))\):
143	the expected-score crossing never understates the expected patch count. One
144	category: \(m^*/n=(1-\varepsilon-v)/(1-v)=8/13\), \(\mathbb E[T]=204/7\).
145	Singleton categories: both equal \(H\), share \(4/25\). *Algebraic identity*,
146	cross-checked by enumerating every patch order on three category shapes and
147	against `ceiling_detection_threshold` and `targeted_ceiling_detection_threshold`.
148	
149	**Proposition 5 (monotonicity of \(m^*\)).** If \(\gamma'\) refines \(\gamma\)
150	then \(m^*(\gamma')\le m^*(\gamma)\) for every failure pattern. *Proof.* Each
151	\(\gamma\)-rate is the size-weighted mean of its \(\gamma'\)-sub-rates, so the
152	\(\gamma\) expected-hit curve is attainable under \(\gamma'\) by proportional
153	(fractional) allocation, and the \(\gamma'\)-greedy curve is at least it.
154	\(\square\) *Algebraic identity*; checked over all 203 maps of \([6]\), 2268
155	refining pairs, 63 patterns, two requirements each.
156	
157	**The stopping time under the static schedule is not monotone.**
158	\(\mathbb E[T]\) under the static greedy schedule can rise along refinement:
159	one block \((4,2)\), \(H=2\), gives \(10/3\); \((2,1),(2,1)\) gives \(7/2\).
160	On \([6]\): record `001101`, \(H=3\), \(21/4\) against \(11/2\). *Finite
161	verified example*, a proof by witness.
162	
163	**Proposition 6 (the optimal adaptive schedule is monotone).** Let
164	\(V^*(\gamma)\) be the minimum, over adaptive policies that re-query the
165	channel after each patch and patch a uniformly random unpatched item of a
166	category they choose, of the expected patches to \(H\) hits. If \(\gamma'\)
167	refines \(\gamma\) then \(V^*(\gamma')\le V^*(\gamma)\).
168	
169	*Proof.* A \(\gamma\)-policy's information, the coarse counts, is a function
170	of the \(\gamma'\)-information, and patching a uniformly random unpatched
171	item of a coarse block is the same as choosing a sub-block with probability
172	proportional to its unpatched items and patching at random there. So every
173	\(\gamma\)-policy is a \(\gamma'\)-policy with the same law of patch
174	outcomes, and the minimum over \(\gamma'\)-policies is no larger. \(\square\)
175	`optimal_adaptive_value` computes \(V^*\) by dynamic programming on the
176	multiset of (remaining, failures) pairs. *Evidence status: algebraic
177	identity*; checked on all 2268 refining pairs of \([6]\), 162 cases each
178	(`greedy_vs_optimal_fixture`).
179	
180	**Greedy is not optimal.** The greedy rule (highest current rate, ties to
181	the smaller category) is one adaptive policy, so \(V^*\le\) greedy \(\le\)
182	static everywhere. It is optimal when one hit remains, since exchanging two
183	adjacent patches in different categories changes only the chance that the
184	first of them ends the run, and when every failure must be hit, since any
185	policy that never patches an exhausted category needs
186	\(\sum_cF_c(n_c+1)/(F_c+1)\) patches, the sum of the last-failure positions.
187	Both are checked exhaustively. It is not optimal in general: with categories
188	\((4,2)\) and \((2,1)\) and two hits needed, greedy patches the smaller
189	category first and needs \(19/6\) patches; patching the larger first needs
190	\(37/12\). On six items greedy is strictly worse in 180 of 32,886 cases; on
191	four and five items it is optimal in every case. The greedy value was
192	monotone on every enumerated refining pair, which Proposition 6 does not
193	imply; what it implies is that the right cost of a leak, the optimal
194	expected stopping time, is monotone everywhere. Chain with block sizes
195	50, 25, 10, 5, 2, 1 and failures at items \(0,4,\dots,48\):
196	\(m^*/n=8/13,7/12,8/15,1/2,8/25,4/25\);
197	\(\mathbb E[T]_{\text{static}}=204/7,201/7,51/2,23,31/2,8\);
198	greedy adaptive \(\approx29.14,25.64,21.17,18,12,8\).
199	
200	## 4. Ledger wrapper
201	
202	`audit_category_ledger` accepts a `category_feedback` event carrying the
203	partition used, records it with its position (`score_only`, `category`,
204	`item_level`), and forwards to `audit_ledger` one `score_query` per block of
205	two or more items plus one `item_feedback` naming the singleton items (a count
206	on a singleton is that item's outcome), so the base access rules apply. An
207	optional declared partition per set bounds the leak in the lattice; a finer
208	event is a recorded breach. `audit_ledger` is wrapped, not edited.
209	
210	## Boundaries
211	
212	Deterministic channels only: a stochastic channel is a Markov kernel, for which
213	the \(\mathrm{TV}\) contraction survives (`_pushforward`) but which has no
214	partition, no lattice position, and no converse of Proposition 1; the Blackwell
215	preorder on kernels is not treated. Items are independent and a patch changes
216	its own item only, which the nearest-neighbour learner in `output/eval_reuse_toys`
217	violated. Greedy ties break by index; \(\mathbb E[T]_{\text{static}}\) depends
218	on that choice when two categories share a rate. The optimal adaptive policy
219	is computed, not characterized: no index rule for it is offered, and the
220	enumerations stop at six items. No model or loop evidence.

1	# The selection gap across generations, exactly
2	
3	Draft 0.1 — 2026-10-12. Companion to `evaluation_feedback_insertions.md`, whose selection law
4	stops at one generation and whose multi-generation rows come from seeded JavaScript. This note
5	replaces the accumulation claim with a finite Markov chain in exact arithmetic. No model is
6	called; nothing here is evidence about any controller. Each result names its evidence level
7	from the calculus card (§11): *algebraic identity* holds for every parameter; *finite verified
8	example* is checked only on the enumerated cells; *synthetic mechanism result* is a property
9	of this toy chain.
10	
11	Source `src/spiral_ln/evaluation_feedback_multigen.py`; 70 tests in `tests/`; receipt
12	`output/evaluation_feedback_multigen/multigen_v0_1.json` (30 checks, source hashes, exact
13	fractions, float renderings under `headline`).
14	
15	```powershell
16	$env:PYTHONPATH = "src"
17	python scripts/verify_evaluation_feedback_multigen.py --output output/evaluation_feedback_multigen/multigen_v0_1.json
18	python -m pytest tests/test_evaluation_feedback_multigen.py -q
19	```
20	
21	## 1. The chain: vertices, edges, policy
22	
23	A reused set of \(n\) items. **State**: the incumbent's realized count \(c\in\{0,\dots,n\}\) on
24	that set. Each generation draws \(K\) candidates i.i.d. and independent of the incumbent,
25	\(C_k\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)\), \(M=\max_k C_k\). **Actions**: accept or reject the best candidate.
26	**Policy**: accept iff \(M>c+t(c)\), \(t:\{0..n\}\to\mathbb N\). **Edges**: \(c\to j\) with
27	probability \(P(M=j)\) for \(j>c+t(c)\); the self-loop carries \(F(c+t(c))^K\), \(F\) the binomial
28	CDF with \(F(j)=1\) for \(j\ge n\). The graph is a DAG of upward edges plus self-loops; its sinks
29	\(\{c:c+t(c)\ge n\}\) are the absorbing states. Initial state \(c_0\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)\).
30	Reported score \(c_G/n\); readout value \(p\); readout gap \(\rho_G=\mathbb E[c_G]/n-p\). In the
31	calculus: \(\operatorname{Repeat}_G\) of one generation with carry map "keep \(c\)", composed
32	with \(\operatorname{Feedback}_{s,\text{score-only}}\) whose consumer selects among candidates.
33	
34	**Gate discretization.** `sim.js` accepts iff \(M>c+z\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}\,n\) with \(p=c/n\), i.e.
35	\(M-c>z\sqrt{c(n-c)/n}\). The difference is an integer \(d\), and \(d>x\) iff
36	\(d\ge\lfloor x\rfloor+1\), so \(t(c)=\lfloor z\sqrt{c(n-c)/n}\rfloor\), computed exactly as
37	\(\lfloor\sqrt{a/b}\rfloor=\mathrm{isqrt}(ab)\,//\,b\). For \(n=16,z=3\):
38	\(t=(0,2,3,4,5,5,5,5,6,5,5,5,5,4,3,2,0)\). Fixture `gate_threshold`, checked by
39	\(t^2\le z^2c(n-c)/n<(t+1)^2\) on every state and against the real-valued rule for every
40	integer \(d\). Algebraic identity.
41	
42	## 2. Naive reuse is a running maximum
43	
44	**Proposition 1.** With \(t\equiv0\), \(c_G=\max(c_0,M_1,\dots,M_G)\), the maximum of \(GK+1\)
45	i.i.d. \(\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)\) draws, so \(\rho_G=\) `selection_inflation(n, GK+1, p).readout_gap`.
46	The initial incumbent is one draw because it is scored on the reused set like every candidate;
47	a *known* count \(c_0\) gives \(\mathbb E[\max(c_0,X)]\), \(X\) the max of \(GK\) draws
48	(`running_max_from_point`). *Proof.* If \(M_g>c_{g-1}\) the policy sets
49	\(c_g=M_g=\max(c_{g-1},M_g)\); otherwise \(c_g=c_{g-1}=\max(c_{g-1},M_g)\). Induct. Algebraic
50	identity. The DP equals the closed form on all 18 null cells (\(n\in\{4,8,16\}\),
51	\(K\in\{1,2,4\}\), \(p\in\{\tfrac12,\tfrac14\}\), \(G=0..20\)); at \(n=2,K=2,G=2\) it equals
52	literal enumeration of all \(2^{10}\) item outcomes.
53	
54	**Consequences.** (i) \(\rho_G\) is non-decreasing in \(G\): a maximum over more draws is
55	pointwise larger. (ii) Increments are non-increasing: \(a_{m+1}-a_m=\mathbb E[(X-M_m)^+]\) with
56	\(M_m\) pointwise non-decreasing in \(m\). (iii) \(P(c_G=n)=1-(1-p^n)^{GK+1}\), so for fixed
57	\(n\) and \(0<p<1\), \(\rho_G\uparrow1-p\): bounded by the lattice, never stationary. These are
58	algebraic identities with the proofs above; the fixture verifies them on the enumerated cells
59	only. *Remark, not verified:* while \(GK\) is large and the maximum is still far from \(n\),
60	the Gaussian extreme-value approximation gives \(\rho_G\approx\sqrt{2\ln(GK+1)\,p(1-p)/n}\).
61	
62	Values at \(p=\tfrac12\) (exact in the receipt). \(n=8,K=2\): \(\rho_1=19305/131072\approx0.1473\),
63	\(\rho_5\approx0.2726\), \(\rho_{10}\approx0.3212\), \(\rho_{20}\approx0.3645\). \(n=16,K=4\):
64	\(0.1440,\ 0.2318,\ 0.2648,\ 0.2947\). \(n=4,K=1\): \(\rho_1=35/256\), the insertions note's
65	two-candidate four-item value, the incumbent being the second candidate.
66	
67	## 3. Fresh blocks
68	
69	**Proposition 2.** (a) If each generation scores incumbent and candidates on a fresh block and
70	reports on a second fresh block, the expected reported score is \(p\) at every generation: the
71	readout block is independent of whatever selected the controller, and under the null every
72	controller has probability \(p\). (b) If it reports on the selection block, the reported count
73	at \(g\ge1\) is \(M\) if \(M>I+t(I)\), else \(I\), with \(I\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)\) the
74	incumbent's fresh count; the law does not depend on \(g\). For \(t\equiv0\) it is \(\max(I,M)\),
75	the maximum of \(K+1\) draws, so the gap equals `selection_inflation(n, K+1, p)` at every
76	\(g\ge1\) and does not accumulate. Both algebraic identities (independence, linearity);
77	verified on 12 cells and by enumeration at \(n=2,K=2\) in both modes. The reused chain
78	coincides with (b) at \(G=1\) for any gate and exceeds it strictly for \(G\ge2\) on every
79	enumerated cell (finite check).
80	
81	## 4. The gate
82	
83	**Proposition 3 (false acceptance).** From state \(c\) the generation accepts with probability
84	\(\alpha(c)=1-F(\min(n,c+t(c)))^K\); under the null every acceptance is false, and the
85	unconditional rate at generation \(g\) is \(\sum_c\pi_{g-1}(c)\alpha(c)\). Algebraic identity.
86	For \(n=16,K=4,z=3\): \(\alpha(8)=1-(1-17/65536)^4\approx1.0\times10^{-3}\); naive \(\approx0.36\).
87	
88	**Proposition 4 (gate dominance, null only).** For any \(t\ge0\), couple the gated and naive
89	chains on the same draws. The gated state always belongs to \(\{c_0,M_1,\dots,M_g\}\), whose
90	maximum is the naive state; hence \(c^t_G\le c^0_G\) pointwise, \(\rho^t_G\le\rho^0_G\), and
91	\(\alpha^t(c)\le\alpha^0(c)\). Algebraic identity by coupling; its hypothesis is that every
92	candidate's law is the same whatever the history, i.e. the null. With true gains it fails and
93	can reverse (§5). Values at \(G=20,p=\tfrac12,n=16,K=4\): naive \(0.2947\); \(z=1\): \(0.2723\);
94	\(z=2\): \(0.2019\); \(z=3\): \(0.1328\); expected false acceptances \(2.34\to0.33\).
95	\(n=8,K=2\): naive \(0.3645\), \(z=3\): \(0.0967\). The gate also creates sinks below the
96	ceiling: for \(n=8,z=3\) states \(4..8\) absorb, so a gated loop freezes; the simulation's
97	GATED arm accepting 0–2% of generations is the same mechanism.
98	
99	## 5. True gains: the drift chain
100

23	per-item overrides, so a patch memorizes an item identifier); `items` (\(D\): `s0,s1` in selection set

25	sets); `judgment` (\(J\): one for the resource, inverted on flipped items, less a cost for choosing

30	Observe (observation-only), Controller, Rescore, Payoff (optionally also installing the utility as the

33	`judgment`, `declarations`, `generation` and writes `pi`, `generation`: item-level access returns the

40	**Proposition 1 (disjoint-update law).** Call a footprint *sound* if the operator changes no field
41	outside \(W\) and the new values of \(W\) are a function of the old values of \(R\). If \(a,b\) have sound
42	footprints with \(W_a\cap(R_b\cup W_b)=\emptyset\) and \(W_b\cap(R_a\cup W_a)=\emptyset\), then \(a;b=b;a\) on every record.
43	
44	*Proof.* Fix \(x\). Fields outside \(W_a\cup W_b\) are untouched in both orders. For \(f\in W_a\): in
45	\(a;b\), \(a\) writes \(f\) from \(x|_{R_a}\) and \(b\) leaves it (\(f\notin W_b\)); in \(b;a\), \(b\)
46	leaves \(R_a\) unchanged (\(W_b\cap R_a=\emptyset\)), so \(a\) writes the same value. Likewise \(W_b\). \(\square\)

48	Boundary: sufficient only, and about the record, not about additivity of behavioural effects (calculus

1	# Proposed AI Safety Millennium Problem Candidates
2	
3	## ASMP-CANDIDATE-SET-v0.1 — Definition draft, 2026-07-18
4	
5	## Status
6	
7	This document defines a proposed set of seven long-horizon mathematical problem
8	candidates for AI safety. It is a research-agenda artifact, not an actual prize
9	announcement and not an assertion that every formulation below is known to be
10	open in every nearby mathematical model. Version 0.1 has undergone an internal
11	hostile audit but has not passed the external field review required for a
12	funded public prize. Each statement is versioned because a change to its
13	objects, quantifiers, adversary, or resolution criterion changes the problem.
14	
15	The word **safety** is never left primitive. Every problem freezes a declared
16	risk, safety predicate, verifier relation, or policy predicate. Solving the
17	mathematics shows what follows from that formal object; it cannot prove that the
18	object captures all human values.
19	
20	## Graduation standard for a Millennium-grade problem
21	
22	A candidate should graduate to public-prize status only after it satisfies all
23	of the following. Inclusion in this v0.1 candidate set does not itself certify
24	that every item is already closed under this standard.
25	
26	1. **Closed formal core.** Objects, domains, encodings, resource bounds,
27	   randomness, adversaries, and quantifier order are explicit.
28	2. **Benchmark independence.** A benchmark may instantiate a problem but does
29	   not define safety, deception, correctness, or capability.
30	3. **Liveness.** The domain contains admissible positive and negative examples.
31	   An inert agent, empty environment class, or oracle verifier cannot solve the
32	   problem by definition.
33	4. **Computability boundary.** Formulations over programs confront Rice-,
34	   halting-, Gödel-, or switched-system undecidability instead of hiding it.
35	5. **Performance floor.** Safety coexists with a frozen nonzero competence or
36	   progress requirement whenever abstention would otherwise solve the problem.
37	6. **Invariance.** Conclusions survive declared coordinate changes, equivalent
38	   encodings, renamings, and implementation refactorings.
39	7. **Robust version.** Exact statements have a finite-precision,
40	   perturbation-stable, or `(epsilon, delta)` counterpart—or explicitly prove
41	   why none can exist.
42	8. **Safety reduction.** The mathematical property has a proved implication for
43	   the declared risk functional. Analogy alone is insufficient.
44	9. **Empirical firewall.** Causal faithfulness, model-class membership,
45	   stationarity, metric choice, and linearization radius are premises to be
46	   checked empirically, not conclusions of the theorem.
47	10. **Two-sided resolution rule.** A constructive theorem, a counterexample to
48	    the complete frozen universal statement, a sharp impossibility theorem, an
49	    undecidability result for the frozen uniform decision family, or an
50	    independence result relative to the declared foundational theory may
51	    resolve the problem. Refuting one proposed criterion does not resolve a
52	    broader classification program unless that criterion is the entire frozen
53	    statement.
54	11. **Novelty boundary.** The statement names the classical results it extends.
55	    Renaming an existing theorem does not count.
56	12. **Independent checkability.** Computer-assisted steps use exact or
57	    interval-certified arithmetic and a separately checkable verifier.
58	
59	Simulation, benchmark performance, asymptotic curve fitting, and failure to
60	find a counterexample can support a conjecture but cannot resolve one of these
61	problems.
62	
63	## The seven problems at a glance
64	
65	| ID | Problem | Mathematical frontier | Primary safety use |
66	|---|---|---|---|
67	| ASMP-1 | Mechanistic Identifiability Modulo Functional Symmetry | causal equivalence and intervention complexity | know when an interpretation names a real manipulable mechanism |
68	| ASMP-2 | Shift-Spanning Safety Certification | minimax generalization under structured environment change | know when evaluations span deployment hazards |
69	| ASMP-3 | The Weak-Verifier Soundness Frontier | complexity theory with noisy semantic judgments | know which superhuman work weaker overseers can soundly judge |
70	| ASMP-4 | Two-Port Evaluator-Relative Confinement | nonlinear control through separately bounded read/write interfaces | know the information capacity required to retain control |
71	| ASMP-5 | Reflective Safety under Open-Ended Self-Modification | proof theory, computability, and adaptive dynamics | know when local update certificates compose through recursive change |
72	| ASMP-6 | Adaptive Semantic Collusion Capacity | information theory with strategic learned channels and active audits | bound covert coordination among monitored agents |
73	| ASMP-7 | Capability Attestability under Compression and Decomposition | statistical experiments, telemetry, and transformation semigroups | know which governance predicates remain verifiable after capability migrates |
74	
75	---
76	
77	# ASMP-1 — Mechanistic Identifiability Modulo Functional Symmetry
78	
79	## Safety question
80	
81	When does an interpretability procedure recover a causal mechanism rather than
82	one of many internally different stories that agree on every measurement it
83	made?
84	
85	## Canonical mathematical setting
86	
87	Let `M` range over a frozen class
88	`C(n,s,d,w,p,F,B,kappa,gamma)` of finite analytic computational structural
89	causal models. Here `n` bounds the number of typed nodes, `s` the number of
90	active edges or local mechanisms, `d` the in-degree, `w` the graph width, and
91	`p` each state-space dimension. The registered mechanism class `F` supplies a
92	covering-number or metric-entropy function, an analytic domain/radius, a norm
93	bound `B`, and a noise model. The constants `kappa>0` and `gamma>0` are minimum
94	observational separation/conditioning and intervention-strength margins. A
95	model contains a directed computation graph, internal state spaces, local
96	mechanisms, and an output variable `Y`.
97	
98	Freeze:
99	
100	- an environment family `E` that supplies input and parent configurations;
101	- an intervention family `I` containing specified activation replacements,
102	  path interventions, and bounded parameter-local transformations;
103	- an observation operator
104	
105	```text
106	O_(E,I)(M) = {all registered observational and interventional laws of M};
107	```
108	
109	- a bounded-complexity high-level abstraction `Q(M)`; and
110	- a declared group action `G x Q(C) -> Q(C)` containing only transformations
111	  that preserve the typed causal object, such as permitted internal coordinate
112	  changes, graph automorphisms, and explicitly modeled redundant realizations.
113	
114	Identifiability means
115	
116	```text
117	O_(E,I)(M) = O_(E,I)(M')  implies  Q(M') is in the G-orbit of Q(M).
118	```
119	
120	The abstraction `Q` must be fixed independently of observational equivalence;
121	defining it to make this implication true would be circular.
122	
123	## Cut-Separation Conjecture
124	
125	For generic models in `C(n,s,d,w,p,F,B,kappa,gamma)`, a bounded-complexity
126	causal abstraction is identifiable modulo `G` if and only if both conditions
127	hold:
128	
129	1. the environments excite every parent configuration needed to distinguish
130	   the registered local mechanism class; and
131	2. the intervention hypergraph separates every minimal causal cut capable of
132	   changing the declared outputs or safety variables.
133	
134	Under these conditions, there is a recovery algorithm whose intervention,
135	sample, and arithmetic complexity is polynomial in the finite structural
136	parameters and in the registered metric entropy, condition number, inverse
137	effect/intervention margins, `log(1/delta)`, and `1/epsilon`. The exact encoding
138	and coefficient bit-complexity are part of `F`; no polynomial claim suppresses
139	them. When either condition fails, there exist non-`G`-equivalent mechanisms
140	whose registered interventional laws are identical, and either the
141	observational-equivalence fiber is positive-dimensional or matching
142	query/sample lower bounds grow superpolynomially in a declared size parameter.
143	
144	“Generic” must be stated algebraically or measure-theoretically. It may not
145	silently mean “all inconvenient counterexamples are excluded.”
146	
147	## What a complete resolution requires
148	
149	A complete resolution must provide all four pieces:
150	
151	1. a maximal or explicitly justified symmetry/equivalence quotient;
152	2. necessary and sufficient intervention/environment conditions;
153	3. a constructive recovery procedure with finite-sample stability bounds; and
154	4. matching indistinguishability or query-complexity lower bounds when the
155	   conditions fail.
156	
157	A valid counterexample resolves the frozen Cut-Separation Conjecture as false.
158	It resolves the broader ASMP-1 classification program only if it also supplies
159	a complete replacement criterion or proves that no computable criterion of the
160	declared form can exist.
161	
162	## Liveness and kill examples
163	
164	- **Positive:** a sparse linear causal network with interventions that isolate
165	  every node and excite every parent configuration is recoverable up to the
166	  declared linear gauge.
167	- **Negative:** if one minimal causal cut is never crossed by an intervention,
168	  two nonisomorphic downstream mechanisms can be substituted behind that cut
169	  without changing any registered observation.
170	- **Gauge trap:** neuron identities, SAE coordinates, or basis vectors cannot be
171	  claimed unique when a permitted basis change leaves all interventional laws
172	  unchanged.
173	- **Vacuity trap:** unrestricted nonlinear alignment maps are excluded because
174	  they can make unrelated systems appear causally aligned.
175	
176	## Existing theory this must exceed
177	
178	Causal representation learning already has strong identifiability results under
179	specific interventions, while unrestricted disentanglement and unrestricted
180	alignments are non-identifiable or vacuous. The unresolved target is the exact
181	recoverable quotient for a known computation with feasible internal
182	interventions, distributed/overcomplete representations, and approximate
183	finite-data guarantees—not “discover that interventions help.”
184	
185	## Safety consequence
186	
187	A solution would tell a control system when an internal feature, circuit, or
188	edit site has a stable causal referent and when multiple incompatible
189	mechanisms remain observationally possible. It would turn mechanistic
190	interpretability from explanatory evidence into a typed identifiability claim,
191	without asserting that the recovered abstraction is itself a complete safety
192	specification.
193	
194	---
195	
196	# ASMP-2 — Shift-Spanning Safety Certification
197	
198	## Safety question
199	
200	When do finitely many training and evaluation environments justify a uniform
201	safety claim over a declared family of deployment shifts?
202	
203	## Canonical mathematical setting
204	
205	Let `M` be a registered class of dominated, quadratic-mean differentiable
206	semiparametric environment families `{P^m_(theta,nu) : m in M}` on a common
207	measurable space. It freezes the common parameterization/transport between
208	tangent spaces, nuisance tangent spaces, nuisance trajectories, support/overlap
209	assumptions, curvature and remainder bounds, and compact deployment set
210	`Theta_adv`. Write `P^m_theta` for the distribution along the registered
211	nuisance trajectory of family `m`. Let `h` be a data-selected policy or monitor,
212	`L_s(h,P)` a bounded safety loss, and `U(h,P)` a utility functional with required
213	floor `u_0>0`.
214	
215	Data `D_src` with registered source sample sizes are available only at
216	`theta_1,...,theta_m`. A certificate must hold uniformly over the true family
217	in `M`. Define the certification goal
218	
219	```text
220	inf_(m in M) Pr_(D_src drawn from family m)[
221	    sup_(theta in Theta_adv) L_s(h(D_src),P^m_theta) <= epsilon
222	    and
223	    inf_(theta in Theta_adv) U(h(D_src),P^m_theta) >= u_0
224	] >= 1-delta
225	```
226	
227	Transport the source score spaces to a registered reference tangent space. Let
228	`S_obs` be the closed span of their statistically identifiable score or
229	causal-shift directions after quotienting nuisance/null directions. Let
230	`T_adv` be the transported tangent cone generated by admissible deployment
231	shifts, quotiented by directions on which both the safety loss and utility are
232	locally constant.
233	
234	## Local Shift-Spanning and Global Continuation Conjectures
235	
236	For the frozen quadratic-mean differentiable experiment, a regular,
237	data-dependent **local first-order** safety certificate exists with finite
238	minimax radius if and only if the pathwise derivatives of the declared safety
239	and utility functionals on `T_adv` factor continuously through the identified
240	score experiment, with a strictly positive conditioning margin on their
241	risk-relevant quotient. This statement is local and semiparametric; it does not
242	claim that tangent spanning is necessary for a separate nonlocal structural
243	robust bound.
244	
245	If an admissible risk-relevant direction is unspanned, two environment families
246	can agree on all source distributions and all registered evaluations yet have
247	different local safety derivatives along that direction. The separate global
248	continuation conjecture asks for necessary and sufficient support, compactness,
249	curvature, topology, and model-uncertainty conditions under which the local
250	certificate extends uniformly over `Theta_adv`. Local tangent coverage alone
251	is explicitly not asserted to be globally sufficient.
252	
253	## What a complete resolution requires
254	
255	1. A necessary-and-sufficient local theorem in the frozen semiparametric model,
256	   with a coordinate-invariant quotient/conditioning statistic.
257	2. A local-to-global theorem stating exactly which curvature, topology, and
258	   support assumptions permit continuation over `Theta_adv`.
259	3. Minimax-optimal sample complexity and simultaneous confidence bounds.
260	4. An active design that selects the next environment/intervention to reduce
261	   the largest uncertified risk direction.
262	5. A matching no-free-lunch result when the model/shift set is unrestricted or
263	   a risk derivative is not identifiable from the source experiment.
264	
265	## Liveness and kill examples
266	
267	- **Positive:** a finite-dimensional exponential or causal family whose source
268	  environments span the adversarial tangent cone with a known Hessian bound.
269	- **Negative:** an unseen binary cause changes the correct safe action but has
270	  identical source marginal laws; no source-only learner can certify both
271	  worlds.
272	- **Inert-policy trap:** the utility floor prevents a policy that always refuses
273	  to act from resolving the problem.
274	- **Post-hoc-metric trap:** `Theta_adv`, its metric, and the curvature bound are
275	  frozen before evaluation outcomes.
276	
277	## Existing theory this must exceed
278	
279	Domain adaptation has impossibility theorems, and invariant learning has both
280	positive results and counterexamples. The missing result is not another domain
281	generalization algorithm. It is a sharp certification boundary—necessary and
282	sufficient coverage of the declared safety-relevant shift directions, with a
283	uniform risk certificate and an optimal experiment-selection rule.
284	
285	## Safety consequence
286	
287	A solution would state when a red-team or evaluation suite spans its claimed
288	deployment threat model, identify the missing direction when it does not, and
289	prevent “many diverse tests passed” from being mistaken for a distribution-free
290	safety guarantee.

294	# ASMP-3 — The Weak-Verifier Soundness Frontier
295	
296	## Safety question
297	
298	Which tasks performed by a stronger, possibly adversarial system can be judged
299	soundly by a substantially weaker verifier using only a small number of noisy
300	human-semantic judgments?
301	
302	## Canonical mathematical setting
303	
304	For input length `n`, freeze a decision relation `R_n`; a public-coin message
305	order and stopping rule; an atomic semantic-query language `A_n` with maximum
306	description length, locality radius, evaluation cost, and a registered family
307	of meaning-preserving query replications; an ideal binary semantic oracle `H`;
308	and a noisy oracle `H_tilde`. The noise model specifies a
309	marginal error bound `eta<1/2` and a complete correlation/adaptivity class;
310	independent errors may not be assumed unless they are part of the model.
311	
312	Two strategic provers have computation budget `T(n)` and the frozen zero-sum
313	payoff induced by completeness/soundness. A verifier has time `s(n)`,
314	semantic-query budget `q(n)`, and transcript budget `B(n)`, with all three
315	intended to be `polylog(T(n))`. Admissible transcript encodings, verifier and
316	prover randomness, and adaptive query access are part of the game. The honest
317	prover must itself have an efficient strategy; unbounded “honesty” does not
318	solve obfuscated arguments.
319	
320	Freeze a decidable syntactic relation
321	`Refute_n(tau,S,b)` saying that atom set `S` with answer vector `b` refutes
322	transcript `tau`. Define the **combinatorial local refutation dimension**
323	`r_R(n)` as
324	
325	```text
326	r_R(n) = max_(false admissible transcript tau)
327	         min{|S| : S is a subset of A_n
328	                   and Refute_n(tau,S,H restricted to S)}.
329	```
330	
331	The inner minimum is infinity if no refuting set exists; the outer maximum is
332	zero if there are no false admissible transcripts.
333	
334	This invariant contains no search or efficiency clause. Efficient location of
335	`S` is a separate condition below. The frozen atom length, locality, and
336	evaluation bounds are intended to rule out one “local” claim encoding the full
337	answer; a complete solution must prove that encoding invariance rather than
338	assume it from syntax alone.
339	
340	Independently of the task, define the semantic-noise amplification profile
341	
342	```text
343	a_H(k) = inf_(registered k-query aggregators A)
344	         sup_(legal correlated error laws) Pr[A answers an atom incorrectly].
345	```
346	
347	The infimum ranges only over meaning-preserving replications allowed by the
348	frozen query language; it cannot replace an atom with a full solution.
349	
350	## Weak-Verifier Characterization Conjecture
351	
352	A task family admits a constant-gap, doubly efficient, noise-robust oversight
353	protocol if and only if:
354	
355	1. its combinatorial local refutation dimension is polylogarithmic in the
356	   prover computation;
357	2. an efficient honest prover can find a local refutation against every
358	   efficient dishonest strategy; and
359	3. for some constant `c>0`, `a_H(polylog(T(n))) <= 1/2-c` with a constructive
360	   aggregator, so the registered correlation model supports a constant gap.
361	
362	The conjecture is a characterization, not a claim that debate always works.
363	Tasks with large or computationally inaccessible refutations should fall
364	outside the class even if a fully informed human could eventually judge them.
365	
366	## What a complete resolution requires
367	
368	1. A formal complexity class for the protocols above and a class equality,
369	   separation, or complete invariant characterizing it.
370	2. A constructive protocol with explicit completeness and soundness against
371	   adaptive, obfuscating provers.
372	3. Matching communication, semantic-query, and honest-prover lower bounds.
373	4. A robust theorem for correlated/noisy semantic judgments.
374	5. A proof that the local-refutation definition is invariant under benign
375	   transcript encodings and cannot hide full verification in one “local” query.
376	
377	## Liveness and kill examples
378	
379	- **Positive:** a long hybrid computation whose false traces have short,
380	  efficiently locatable formal-plus-semantic refutations, with semantic atoms
381	  repeated through a registered block-independent noise model that admits
382	  amplification.
383	- **Negative:** a task in which two candidate worlds generate identical allowed
384	  semantic queries but require opposite answers.
385	- **Recomputation trap:** verifier cost must remain asymptotically below solving
386	  the task independently.
387	- **Specification trap:** the theorem certifies relation `R`; it does not prove
388	  that `R` captures human intent.
389	- **Classical-theorem trap:** merely restating `IP=PSPACE`, PCP, or ordinary
390	  verifiable computation does not resolve noisy semantic oversight.
391	
392	## Existing theory this must exceed
393	
394	Interactive proofs show remarkable verification power for formal languages,
395	and doubly efficient debate has positive results for computations with
396	black-box human-judgment queries. The open frontier is efficient honest
397	refutation under obfuscation, noisy/correlated semantic judgments, and tasks for
398	which no short human-verifiable transcript is given in advance.
399	
400	## Safety consequence
401	
402	A solution would partition tasks into those that can be soundly delegated to
403	superhuman systems with bounded oversight and those for which debate,
404	consultancy, amplification, or decomposition cannot supply the claimed
405	guarantee without stronger verification primitives.
406

409	# ASMP-4 — Two-Port Evaluator-Relative Confinement
410	
411	## Safety question
412	
413	How much information must independently cross the observation and actuation
414	interfaces to keep an adaptive system inside a declared evaluator-safe region?
415	
416	## Canonical mathematical setting
417	
418	Consider an uncertain controlled process
419	
420	```text
421	x_(t+1) = F(x_t,u_t,w_t),
422	```
423	
424	with disturbance `w_t`, initial set `K_0`, and evaluator-safe target `K`. For a
425	registered causal code `C` and horizon `T`, let `M_r^C(T)` and `M_w^C(T)` be
426	finite transcript alphabets, or prefix-free countable alphabets charged by
427	worst-case length. Define its worst-case asymptotic achieved rates
428	
429	```text
430	r_r(C) = limsup_(T->infinity) (1/T) log2 |M_r^C(T)|,
431	r_w(C) = limsup_(T->infinity) (1/T) log2 |M_w^C(T)|.
432	```
433	
434	A causal sensor encoder emits only the read transcript; a controller receives
435	only those symbols and emits the write transcript; an actuator decoder maps
436	write symbols to controls. Variable-length variants must charge prefix-free
437	worst-case or expected length explicitly rather than reuse these definitions.
438	
439	The plant, sensor, controller, and actuator are separate components. No analog
440	state, shared object reference, common random variable correlated with the
441	state, or uncharged side channel may cross either interface. Internal memory,
442	delays, block coding, and shared randomness independent of the plant state are
443	explicit parts of the architecture.
444	
445	Define the achievable safety-capacity region
446	
447	```text
448	R_K = {(R_r,R_w): there exists a registered causal code C with
449	                   r_r(C) <= R_r and r_w(C) <= R_w
450	                   such that every x_0 in K_0 remains in K
451	                   for every allowed disturbance sequence}.
452	```
453	
454	When only an evaluator output must remain safe, motion tangent to safe fibers
455	or the boundary may be quotiented out. The required invariant must distinguish
456	full-state entropy from evaluator-transversal entropy.
457	
458	## Two-Port Capacity Conjecture
459	
460	For a registered normally hyperbolic, locally controllable class with bounded
461	uncertainty, delay, memory, control-authority, and disturbance conventions, the
462	closure of `R_K` has a variational characterization in terms of two possibly
463	different evaluator-transversal invariance quantities:
464	
465	```text
466	R_r >= h_read_perp,
467	R_w >= h_write_perp,
468	```
469	
470	together with any architecture-dependent tradeoff inequalities. Read-only
471	specializations must recover the classical sum of positive evaluator-normal
472	Lyapunov exponents under the assumptions of the corresponding data-rate
473	theorem. No equality is assumed for the write port merely from full
474	controllability: determining when `h_write_perp` equals, exceeds, or is
475	incomparable to the read threshold is part of the problem. Tangential
476	instability costs rate only insofar as the frozen dynamics couple it into
477	evaluator-relevant directions.
478	
479	The conjecture does **not** assume the region is rectangular in general.
480	Decoder memory, predictive control, block coding, and side information can
481	change the write-side frontier and must be included in the theorem.
482	
483	## What a complete resolution requires
484	
485	1. A coordinate-invariant definition of the read and write transversal
486	   entropies.
487	2. A variational formula for the entire achievable rate region, not only one
488	   lower bound.
489	3. Converse theorems and constructive coder-controller/actuator schemes.
490	4. Exact finite-horizon corrections showing how initial safety margin permits
491	   temporary operation below the asymptotic rate.
492	5. Counterexamples locating the boundary of partial observability,
493	   uncertainty, nonhyperbolicity, and side-information assumptions.
494	
495	## Liveness and kill examples
496	
497	- **Positive:** a stable plant with adequate control authority may need zero
498	  asymptotic rate.
499	- **Negative:** an unstable evaluator-normal mode with a positive-volume initial
500	  collar cannot be confined below its information-expansion rate.
501	- **Authority control:** a full-state/full-action controller distinguishes
502	  information failure from insufficient actuator authority.
503	- **Split-port witness:** in a registered mode-switching plant, hold the sensor
504	  experiment fixed while varying the finite actuator dictionary needed to
505	  counter distinct modes; the write boundary changes without changing the read
506	  boundary.
507	- **Side-channel control:** supplying uncharged analog state must alter the
508	  threshold, demonstrating why the architectural separation is load-bearing.
509	- **Monte Carlo trap:** random nonfailure cannot establish universal
510	  confinement.
511	
512	## Existing theory this must exceed
513	
514	Data-rate theorems, invariance entropy, uncertain-system feedback entropy, and
515	output invariance entropy already exist. Re-proving `sum log |lambda|` for a
516	single linear channel is not a solution. The missing object is the joint
517	two-interface capacity region for nonlinear uncertain output/evaluator
518	confinement, including the quotient/transversal and finite-horizon terms.
519	
520	## Safety consequence
521	
522	A solution would convert “monitoring and intervention are sufficiently rich”
523	into separate, auditable interface requirements. It would also identify when a
524	governance or control proposal fails because the controller cannot observe
525	enough, cannot write enough, or is measuring instability irrelevant to the
526	declared evaluator boundary.
527

530	# ASMP-5 — Reflective Safety under Open-Ended Self-Modification
531	
532	## Safety question
533	
534	Can local certificates remain sound through an unbounded sequence of
535	self-modifications that changes not only behavior but also the proposer,
536	evaluator, or certificate-producing machinery, while retaining nontrivial
537	progress?
538	
539	## Canonical mathematical setting
540	
541	A system state is `z=(p,T,c)`, consisting of an executable program or policy
542	`p`, a proof/certificate system `T`, and its control state `c`. An allowed
543	update `F` may replace any declared subset of these objects. Freeze:
544	
545	- a formal language and operational semantics;
546	- a semantic safety set `S` or trace property;
547	- a competence/progress index `P` with a nonzero floor;
548	- an effectively presented update grammar `U`;
549	- a computable local certificate relation `Cert(z,F,pi)`; and
550	- a trusted base semantics/kernel describing which part, if any, cannot be
551	  rewritten, with soundness stated as an assumption rather than self-certified.
552	
553	The desired soundness property is
554	
555	```text
556	z_(t+1) = F_t(z_t), z_0 in S, and Cert(z_t,F_t,pi_t) for every t
557	implies z_t in S for every t,
558	```
559	
560	for every adaptive certified update sequence. Nontriviality requires a uniform
561	update generator over a registered infinite task family, infinitely many
562	behaviorally nonequivalent certified states, and unbounded cumulative progress
563	under the frozen index. Identity updates, a single whitelisted infinite chain,
564	or positive increments with bounded Zeno sum do not count.
565	
566	## Reflective Safety Frontier Problem
567	
568	Let one regime reduce to another when there is a computable, safety- and
569	progress-preserving translation of its language, update grammar, and
570	certificates. Characterize the resulting positive/negative frontier of regimes
571	for which a computable certificate architecture can simultaneously satisfy:
572	
573	1. uniform semantic soundness for all adaptive certified sequences;
574	2. compositionality when the proposer and certificate generator are replaced;
575	3. an explicit corrigibility/interruption condition;
576	4. perturbation robustness or probabilistic failure bounds; and
577	5. open-ended nontrivial progress.
578	
579	No unique greatest regime is assumed; incomparable frontier components and a
580	proof that no greatest effective class exists are allowed outcomes. The
581	canonical unrestricted quantifier order is: for every total computable
582	certificate architecture `A` and every nontrivial extensional trace property
583	`S`, if `A` is uniformly sound over all partial-computable update programs, then
584	`A` fails the registered uniform open-ended-progress condition on some task
585	family. The canonical dichotomy conjecture is:
586	
587	- no such architecture exists for all partial computable self-modifiers and any
588	  nontrivial extensional semantic safety property; but
589	- a nontrivial downward-closed positive region exists for proof-carrying updates
590	  that preserve an inductive invariant in an assumed-sound fixed kernel, or in
591	  a precisely characterized hierarchy of reflective proof systems.
592	
593	The problem is to locate the exact frontier, not to assume a differentiable
594	“self-improvement Jacobian.”
595	
596	## What a complete resolution requires
597	
598	1. A matching impossibility theorem for the unrestricted computable class,
599	   identifying the exact diagonalization, Rice, Löb, or consistency barrier.
600	2. Nontrivial positive constructions and a characterization of the effective
601	   frontier, including whether a greatest positive regime exists.
602	3. A proof that certificates compose through permitted verifier/evaluator
603	   changes rather than only through fixed-policy updates.
604	4. A performance theorem excluding inert or finitely terminating solutions.
605	5. A robust stochastic/finite-precision counterpart or a proof that one is
606	   impossible.
607	
608	## Liveness and kill examples
609	
610	- **Positive:** proof-carrying finite-state or polynomial updates preserving a
611	  common inductive barrier in a frozen checker.
612	- **Reflective positive target:** a stratified proof-system hierarchy in which
613	  permitted verifier replacements compose through an assumed-sound root
614	  semantics while generating infinitely many behaviorally nonequivalent safe
615	  states.
616	- **Negative:** arbitrary programs whose “safe forever” predicate encodes the
617	  halting problem.
618	- **Löb trap:** a theory cannot be assumed to prove the soundness of an
619	  arbitrarily stronger successor merely because the successor says it is sound.
620	- **Spectral trap:** a local spectral radius cannot replace nonlinear,
621	  adaptive, or switched-system safety; boundedness of arbitrary matrix products
622	  is already undecidable in broad classes.
623	- **Channel trap:** proposal-channel recursion under a frozen scorer does not
624	  establish evaluator- or objective-channel recursion.
625	
626	## Existing theory this must exceed
627	
628	Reflective oracles, Löbian obstacles, proof-carrying code, inductive invariants,
629	barrier certificates, and self-modifying-agent models supply important partial
630	constructions. Conversely, computability and switched-system results establish
631	hard impossibility boundaries. The unresolved target is the effective robust
632	frontier allowing both compositional safety and open-ended certified change.
633	
634	## Safety consequence
635	
636	A solution would state exactly which recursive training or self-editing systems
637	can inherit safety from local update checks, where an immutable root of trust is
638	mathematically necessary, and which broader claims cannot be certified even in
639	principle.
640
